---
title: "Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

This is the 12-bar blues from the drum chair, starting with nothing but the beat. You need
to be able to hit the ride cymbal (or hi-hat), the snare and the bass drum, and to work the
hi-hat pedal. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see
[Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues](blues-changes.qmd).

**How to use the page.** Every step has two bars of the beat written large, a chord chart,
and the whole chorus written on a drum staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the
notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that
is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick **Drums alone** to hear the drummer without the
bass and piano, and **Leave out the drums** to take over. Each step starts in its own feel
and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.

## Reading a drum part

Each line or space of the staff is one part of the kit. Cymbals and anything struck on the
rim are written with an ✕. What the hands play has stems up; what the feet play has stems
down. **Click a piece to hear it**: the picture shows where each one is written, and the
line under it has the same notes in the same places, so you can click those too. Hover over
any drum note on this page and it tells you which piece it is.

<div class="bl-drumkit"></div>

<div class="bl-drumkey"></div>

## 1. The beat and the form

A drummer has two jobs on a blues: keep the time, and know where in the twelve bars the
band is. Start with the plainest time there is. The ride cymbal (or the closed hi-hat)
plays all four beats. The left foot closes the hi-hat on **2 and 4**. Nothing else.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="quarters"></div>

Count the bars out loud while you play: four bars, then four more, then the last four. The
chords change at bar 5, bar 7 and bar 9. Listen for the bass moving and learn to hear those
moments coming.

## 2. The ride pattern

Swing time on the ride cymbal is the four beats plus a *skip note* just before beats 3 and
1: **ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a**. It is written as two eighth notes, but the first is
long and the second short, as if the beat were divided in three and you played the first
and last parts. Keep the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="ride"></div>

Listen with **Drums alone** to hear how late the skip note sits. Slow the tempo down and
it gets later still.

## 3. Swing time

Now the other two limbs. In swing the bass drum is played very quietly on all four beats,
felt more than heard (*feathering*), and it is not written. The snare does not keep time:
it answers the band with a note here and there, often on the last part of a beat. The
band's drummer improvises this, so the notation changes every chorus.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="time"></div>

Start with the ride pattern and the hi-hat foot. Add one snare note per bar, on the "a" of
beat 4, and leave it at that until it is comfortable.

## 4. Showing the form

A fill tells the band where it is. On a blues the places to mark are the ends of the three
four-bar phrases: **bar 4**, which leads to the IV chord; **bar 8**, which leads to the last
line; and **bar 12**, which leads back to the top. The small ones need only a beat or two.
The one in bar 12 can be bigger, and the crash on beat 1 of the next chorus is its landing.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="fills"></div>

Keep the time going right up to the fill and come out of it on beat 1. A fill that loses
the beat is worse than no fill.

## 5. The shuffle

The beat of Chicago blues. The cymbal plays the swung eighths all the way through, long,
short, long, short, with the bass drum on 1 and 3 and a full snare on **2 and 4**. This is
the first beat on this page with a backbeat.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="shuffle"></div>

## 6. The slow blues in 12/8

At a slow tempo every beat divides in three, and the cymbal plays all three parts. Kick on
1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. It is written here in 4/4 with triplets; the same beat is often
written in 12/8.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="slow"></div>

## 7. Straight eighths

Not every blues swings. In a boogaloo or a rock blues the eighth notes are even. The cymbal
plays eight to the bar, the bass drum is on 1 and 3, and the left hand plays a cross-stick
on 2 and 4.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="straight"></div>

## 8. Grabbing the crash

A crash cymbal rings for a long time. Sometimes you want the accent without the ring: hit the
crash, then catch its edge with the other hand straight away, so that it stops. Drummers call
this a *choke*. It is written as a short crash with **choke** over it.

Here the band plays the straight-eighths beat from step 7 with a small fill at the end of bars 4
and 8, and the crash is grabbed on beat 1 of **bar 5** and **bar 9**, the first bar of the second
and third lines. Hit the crash together with the bass drum, and have the hand on the cymbal
before beat 2. Then go straight back to the time. When the band stops at the end, the last
crash is grabbed too.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="grab"></div>

Try it with the loop on and listen to the gap the choke leaves. A grabbed crash says "here"
louder than a ringing one, because of the silence after it.

## 9. A tune: Blues in the Closet

Oscar Pettiford's riff blues, at a medium swing. The melody is one two-bar riff played
three times, and each time it ends on a long note, in bars 4, 8 and 12. Those are the same
three places step 4 marked with fills. The tune leaves the space; the drummer fills it and
sets up the next phrase.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="fills" data-chart="closet" data-tune="closet"></div>

Play time through the riff and stay out of its way: no snare on top of the melody's
accents. Read the melody while you play. A drummer who knows the tune plays the form
without counting.

## Where to go next

- Loop each step with the drums left out and play it for ten choruses without losing the
  form.
- Play the fills step with your own fills in bars 4, 8 and 12.
- Take a chorus from [the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd): the busier the chords, the
  more the band needs the form marked clearly.
- **Tools → Backing Track** has every groove on this page, and many others, under any tune.
